cues.text: Chapter nine.
Worked archived CA questions.
In this chapter we turn from principles to practice.
We are going to work through problems that were submitted in earlier continuous assessments, known as CA, and see how the legal reasoning behind each answer is built.
Before we begin, a few points about how this material is presented.
The problems you will meet here are paraphrases of the submitted CA problems.
They are not word-for-word copies of the originals.
Each problem keeps its identifier, its ID, so you can trace it back to the archived question it came from.
Each also keeps its provisional answer letter.
The word provisional matters.
These letters are the answers as they currently stand in the archive, and you should treat them as provisional rather than as final, confirmed answers.
One more point.
The original multiple-choice options are not reproduced in this chapter.
So you will not see the full list of lettered choices for each question.
Instead, the emphasis is on the explanation: for each problem, we explain the legal reasoning that supports the answer letter.
Your goal is to understand why an answer is reasoned the way it is, so that you can apply the same reasoning to a differently worded question in an assessment.
A good habit as you study each worked problem is to ask the same questions every time.
Who are the parties involved?
What interests and duties do they have?
Which legal rule, or which ethical principle, actually applies?
And is the point being tested a matter of enforceable law, or a matter of ethics, professional codes or organisational policy?
Keeping those categories separate is one of the most useful skills in this course.
With that approach in mind, we are ready to begin working through the archived problems, one at a time, in the order they appear.
